questions.q: What does the --coverage-formatters flag on sf project deploy start do?
options: It deletes existing code coverage data from the org
It emits code coverage data in a specified format (e.g. json), and can be repeated to emit more than one format
It sets the minimum required coverage percentage
It disables Apex tests entirely
questions.explain: --coverage-formatters controls the output format of coverage data, useful for later pipeline steps that parse it for dashboards or gates; it can be repeated for multiple formats.

questions.q: Why do CI pipelines often raise --wait above its 33-minute default for a production-bound deploy?
options: Because --wait has no default and must always be set
Because GitHub Actions jobs always time out after exactly 33 minutes
Because --wait controls how many Apex tests run
Because a large deployment running RunLocalTests can legitimately take longer than 33 minutes, and pipelines don't want a slow run cut off mid-deploy
questions.explain: The CLI's default wait is 33 minutes; a pipeline deploying a large org with full local tests may need more time, so teams often raise --wait explicitly rather than risk a cutoff.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a CI pipeline should always set an explicit --target-org rather than relying on a default org?
options: Because the concept of a locally-set default org doesn't exist cleanly on a disposable CI runner that starts fresh every run, so the target must be explicit
Because --target-org disables Apex testing
Because explicit target orgs run faster than default orgs
There is no real reason, it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: A CI runner has no persistent local state between runs, so there's no implicit 'default org' to fall back on -- the authentication step must set an explicit, named alias.

questions.q: Mechanically, how does a failing Apex test inside a deploy command end up blocking a pull request?
options: GitHub emails the repository owner manually
The deploy command silently ignores test failures
The deploy command exits with a non-zero status, GitHub Actions stops the job and marks the run red, and a required check then blocks the PR merge
Apex test failures have no effect on the CLI's exit code
questions.explain: A non-zero exit code from the deploy step is what GitHub Actions uses to fail the job; if that check is required for merge via branch protection, the PR is blocked.

questions.q: What does setting continue-on-error: true on a deploy step do, and why is it almost never appropriate there?
options: It lets the job proceed to later steps even if the deploy step fails, which defeats the deploy step's purpose as a gate
It makes the deploy run twice for safety
It automatically fixes any failed Apex tests
It has no effect on step behavior
questions.explain: continue-on-error overrides the normal fail-the-job behavior on a failing step -- exactly the opposite of what you want from a deploy step meant to gate the rest of the pipeline.
